newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico clamps down on security as Clinton visits.
newsitem.headline: Mexico clamps down on security as Clinton visits.

text.p: Armed troops and police threw a tight security cordon around one of Mexico's plushest suburbs on Monday in an unprecedented crackdown hours before the arrival of U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Police manning white barriers peered into cars, baby strollers and designer handbags as locals entered the up-scale hotel district of Polanco where Clinton will stay until Wednesday in his first state visit to Mexico.
Camouflaged troops bearing automatic rifles and fixed gazes stood in stark contrast to bemused market vendors at Polanco's fruit stalls.
"This is an exaggeration, I've never seen security like this," said Sergio Villanueva, a flower vendor whose van full of roses was searched early on Monday as he entered Polanco.

"If there was any problems it would be against our own government, not Clinton. But here there are no terrorists, we are not in Lima," he added, referring to the Peruvian embassy hostage crisis which ended last month.

The preventive measures reflected the Mexican government's desire to avoid any embarrassing anti-American dissent during Clinton's visit. Dispute over drug trafficking and illegal immigration have soured U.S.-Mexican relations recently.
Trying to give the impression of normal life, authorities did what they could to minimise the heavy security presence.
Busloads of riot police sat quietly in leafy sidestreets, smoke billowing out of air vents in the roof as their occupants chain-smoked cigarettes and played cards.
One trooper told Reuters that dozens more security personnel were deployed in plain clothes and would be alerted by radio if there were any protests.
"I doubt there will be any riots, but if there are, we're ready," he said.

At the U.S. Embassy where protests were expected Tuesday, scores of unarmed policewomen with white hats and clipboards were on guard, replacing the usual tough-looking riot police with their batons and shields.

"Our work is 100 percent social," said Maria del Pilar Perez Rodriguez, a smiling policewoman at the embassy. "They don't want the riot police because they give the impression of aggression and conflict."
The government also appeared to be carefully avoiding any potential flashpoints for its citizens, many of whom have been angered recently by a U.S. crackdown on illegal immigration.
